readerTitle: Why the product with the best margin can lose the shelf
caseNote: 가상 사례 (철물점 계산대 선반, 대기업 사내 개발팀) + 실제 관찰 (소매업의 면적당 매출 지표) · 모든 수치는 설명용
insight: 무엇이 부족한지 먼저 찾고, 모든 선택지를 그 부족한 자원 한 단위가 벌어들이는 돈으로 비교한다.
misconception: 마진이 가장 높은 제품, 가치가 가장 큰 프로젝트를 고르면 된다. 희소성은 돈이 부족할 때만의 문제다.

sources.text: 관리회계의 표준 개념 (제약 자원 단위당 공헌이익으로 순위 매기기)
소매업의 일반적 성과 지표 (면적당 매출, sales per square foot)

factChecks.note: 선반 계산: 양초 2개 × $12 = 피트당 주 $24, 충전기 10개 × $4 = $40, 건전지 20개 × $1.50 = $30. 10피트 기준 각각 주 $240, $400, $300. 모두 가상 수치입니다.
사내 팀 계산: 통합 $120k ÷ 6주 = 주당 $20k, 온보딩 수정 $40k ÷ 1주 = $40k, 리포트 $45k ÷ 2주 = $22.5k, 보관 자동화 $60k ÷ 3주 = $20k. 작은 세 개 합계 1 + 2 + 3 = 6주, $40k + $45k + $60k = $145k. 모두 가상 수치입니다.
'소매업체들이 오래전부터 면적당 매출을 추적해 왔다'는 일반적 관찰로만 적었습니다. 특정 기업이나 수치는 인용하지 않았습니다.
레스토랑 예시(긴 코스 요리가 빠른 회전 메뉴보다 덜 벌 수 있다)는 가능성으로만 표현한 설명용 예시입니다.

cards.title: Why the product with the best margin can lose the shelf
body: A candle earns the store $12. A phone charger earns $4.
Both want the same small shelf by the checkout. The obvious pick is the candle. The shelf disagrees.

image.label: A short checkout shelf with candles, chargers and batteries competing for space
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 계산대 옆 좁은 선반 하나에 양초, 휴대폰 충전기, 건전지 상자가 서로 밀치며 자리를 차지하려는 장면. 선반 위에 줄자가 놓여 있음. 실제 브랜드 로고나 상표는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: Who gets the shelf?
body: You run a hardware store with 10 feet of shelf by the checkout. Profit here means what's left after the product's cost.
Each week, one foot of shelf sells: 2 candles at $12 profit each, or 10 chargers at $4, or 20 packs of batteries at $1.50. Which product gets the whole shelf?

options.text: Candles: the highest profit per item
options.feedback: You win on every single sale but lose on space. Candles sell slowly, so each foot earns only $24 a week.

options.text: Chargers: the middle profit, but fast sellers
options.feedback: Each foot earns $40 a week, the most of the three. You give up big wins per sale to earn more from the shelf itself.

options.text: Batteries: they sell the most units
options.feedback: Good instinct to look at speed, not just margin. But units aren't profit: each foot earns $30, less than chargers.

cards.title: Measure by the foot, not by the item.
body: Across all 10 feet: candles earn **$240** a week, chargers **$400**. The best margin per item earns the least per foot.

cards.title: Scarcity
body: **Scarcity** means you want more than you have. Every business has something it can't quickly get more of: shelf space, staff hours, cash, seats, machine time.

The twist: once something is scarce, judge each option by what it earns *per unit of that scarce thing*. Here the scarce thing is shelf, so the right number is **profit per foot**, not profit per sale.

image.label: Three products ranked by profit per foot instead of profit per item
image.brief: 인포그래픽. 왼쪽은 '개당 이익' 기준 순위(양초 1위), 오른쪽은 '선반 1피트당 이익' 기준 순위(충전기 1위). 가운데 화살표로 순위가 뒤집히는 모습 강조. 로고 없음.

cards.title: Find the bottleneck first.
body: Ask one question: if I had more of one thing tomorrow, what would grow profit most? That thing is your scarce resource.
Retailers have long tracked sales per square foot for this reason. Accountants use the same method for factories: rank products by margin per unit of the limited resource, such as machine hours.
Things you have plenty of don't deserve the same attention. Measure everything against the one that's short.
cards.softwareNote: In software, the scarce thing is often engineering time, or space on a screen your users actually look at. A feature's total value matters less than its value per week of building.

cards.title: Every business has its own shelf.
body: The scarce thing changes by business. The method doesn't.
list: **Restaurant on Friday night:** seats per hour. A long tasting menu can earn less than quicker meals.
**Consultant:** billable hours. A small client can pay more per hour than a big one.
**Workshop:** machine time on the busiest machine.
**Delivery van:** space in the back on each route.
cards.callout: Name the shelf, then count per foot of it.

cards.title: Per-foot numbers don't stay fixed.
body: The first foot of chargers may sell 10 a week. The tenth foot may sell two. Customers only need so many, so test before giving everything to the winner.
The scarce thing also moves. Fill the shelf well and the limit may become cash or staff time.
And some value hides from per-foot math. A product that draws people in may sell other things on the way out.

cards.title: Now it's a team inside a big company.
body: You lead an internal tools team at a large logistics company. You have 6 engineer-weeks left this quarter. Estimated yearly savings:

options.text: Build the integration: the single biggest win
options.feedback: It's the biggest project, but it earns $20k per week of your scarce time. It uses the whole quarter for $120k.
Same 6 weeks, about $145k. You trade one headline win for more value per week, but check whether the estimates are solid.

options.text: Ask for more engineers before choosing
options.feedback: Worth raising for next quarter. New people rarely add capacity this quarter, so you still have to choose.

cards.title: Find what's scarce, then measure everything per unit of it.
body: The best option per sale or per project is often not the best use of the thing you're short on.
**Try it today:** name the one thing your business most needs more of this month. Rank your top three products or projects by what each earns per unit of it.
